claims.claim_text: A global retail company used AWS EKS for storefronts, kept inventory on-prem for sub-5 ms scanners, and ran isolated cloud/on-prem platforms for two years.
claims.anchor_text: A global retail company ran customer-facing applications on AWS EKS but kept inventory management on-premises due to latency requirements -- warehouse scanners needed sub-5ms response times. For two years, their cloud and on-prem clusters operated as isolated islands with separate CI/CD pipelines, monitoring, service discovery, and network policies.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A hybrid retail architecture can place latency-sensitive inventory systems on-premises while customer-facing services run in a public cloud, creating separate delivery, monitoring, discovery, and policy surfaces if connectivity is not designed as a shared platform.
claims.rationale: This is an unattributed war story with fake-precise timing and latency details.

claims.claim_text: The same unnamed company took six weeks to build fragile public endpoints, saw 40-400 ms latency, and suffered a 45-minute Black Friday outage from an ISP BGP route leak.
claims.anchor_text: When a product launch required real-time inventory checks from the cloud storefront to the on-prem API, the team patched together public internet endpoints and manual firewall rules. It took six weeks and was fragile -- response times varied 40-400ms. During Black Friday, a BGP route leak by an upstream ISP made the endpoint unreachable for 45 minutes. The storefront showed "out of stock" for items sitting in warehouses.
claims.suggested_rewrite: When cloud services need real-time access to on-premises APIs, ad hoc public endpoints and manual firewall rules can create fragile paths that fail under routing, latency, or availability pressure.
claims.rationale: The outage, timing, latency range, and business symptom are presented as a real incident but have no attributable source.

claims.claim_text: The unnamed company later spent three months on Direct Connect, WireGuard, Submariner, and Istio, then achieved incident-free Black Friday and consistent 8 ms inventory latency.
claims.anchor_text: The company then invested three months in proper hybrid connectivity: a dedicated interconnect, WireGuard tunnels, Submariner for cross-cluster service discovery, and Istio for unified traffic management. The next Black Friday ran without incident. Inventory API latency was a consistent 8ms. This architectural transformation underscores why robust hybrid connectivity design is a core requirement rather than an operational afterthought.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A planned hybrid connectivity layer can combine private interconnects, encrypted tunnels, cross-cluster service discovery, and service-mesh policy so teams are not relying on one-off network exceptions during high-traffic events.
claims.rationale: This continues the same unattributed war story and includes fake-precise implementation duration and latency.

claims.claim_text: The VPN comparison table claims WireGuard is about 4,000 lines while IPsec is about 400,000 lines.
claims.anchor_text: | **Code complexity** | ~4,000 lines | ~400,000 lines |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Implementation surface** | Smaller, modern codebase | Mature protocol family with many implementations |
claims.rationale: The exact cross-implementation code-size comparison is not stable or directly supportable.

claims.claim_text: The VPN comparison table gives exact per-core throughput ranges for WireGuard and IPsec.
claims.anchor_text: | **Performance** | 1.0-3.0 Gbps per core | 0.5-1.60 Gbps per core |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Performance** | Benchmark on your hardware and kernel | Benchmark on your appliance, cipher suite, and offload path |
claims.rationale: The exact throughput ranges depend heavily on hardware, kernel, cipher suite, packet size, and offload.

claims.claim_text: The VPN comparison table gives exact latency overhead ranges for WireGuard and IPsec.
claims.anchor_text: | **Latency overhead** | ~0.5ms | ~1-2ms |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Latency overhead** | Measure on the target path | Measure on the target path |
claims.rationale: The exact millisecond overheads are unsourced benchmark numbers.

claims.claim_text: WireGuard has built-in key rotation every two minutes.
claims.rationale: The WireGuard protocol page is the appropriate primary source, but wireguard.com is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN supports large-bandwidth tunnels up to 5 Gbps and VPN connections have two IPsec tunnels.
claims.rationale: AWS VPN quotas document standard and large-bandwidth tunnel limits and related tunnel quotas.

claims.claim_text: AWS Transit Gateway VPN attachments remain limited to 1.25 Gbps per VPN connection.
claims.anchor_text: Note that AWS Transit Gateway VPN attachments remain limited to 1.25 Gbps per VPN connection.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Check the current AWS VPN quotas before assuming a Transit Gateway VPN attachment is limited to the older standard tunnel rate.
claims.rationale: Current AWS documentation lists large-bandwidth VPN tunnel options, so this dated limitation is unsafe.

claims.claim_text: Azure Virtual WAN site-to-site VPN supports 20 Gbps aggregate throughput, 2 Gbps per VPN connection, 1 Gbps per tunnel, and single TCP flows above 1.5 Gbps may degrade.
claims.rationale: Azure service limits list Virtual WAN VPN aggregate and per-connection throughput limits.

claims.claim_text: Google Cloud HA VPN supports approximately 1-3 Gbps or 250,000 packets per second per tunnel, and 99.99% SLA requires HA topology configuration.
claims.rationale: Google Cloud HA VPN topology and bandwidth documentation covers tunnel throughput and SLA topology requirements.

claims.claim_text: WireGuard AllowedIPs acts as both access control and routing selection for tunnel traffic.
claims.rationale: WireGuard's cryptokey routing documentation directly explains AllowedIPs, but the official domain is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN MTU is 1446 bytes with MSS 1406, while Transit Gateway supports 8500-byte MTU for VPC, Direct Connect, Connect, and peering attachments.
claims.rationale: AWS customer gateway best practices document the VPN MTU/MSS values; Transit Gateway MTU is documented in AWS Transit Gateway concepts.

claims.claim_text: The interconnect comparison table claims all three providers typically deliver less than 5 ms latency.
claims.anchor_text: | **Latency** | <5ms typical | <5ms typical | <5ms typical |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Latency** | Location- and carrier-dependent; measure the path | Location- and carrier-dependent; measure the path | Location- and carrier-dependent; measure the path |
claims.rationale: The exact latency target is topology-specific and not a provider-wide fact.

claims.claim_text: The interconnect comparison table gives exact setup windows of 2-4 weeks for AWS/Azure and 1-3 weeks for GCP.
claims.anchor_text: | **Setup time** | 2-4 weeks | 2-4 weeks | 1-3 weeks |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Setup time** | Depends on provider, carrier, partner, facility, and cross-connect process | Depends on provider, carrier, partner, facility, and cross-connect process | Depends on provider, carrier, partner, facility, and cross-connect process |
claims.rationale: Provisioning duration is not a stable provider fact and varies by facility and partner.

claims.claim_text: The interconnect comparison table lists approximate monthly 10G port costs for AWS, Azure, and GCP.
claims.suggested_rewrite: | **Monthly cost (10G)** | Varies by region, port speed, data transfer, and partner charges | Varies by region, circuit/SKU, data transfer, and partner charges | Varies by region, attachment, egress, and partner charges |
claims.rationale: Exact cloud connectivity prices change and depend on region, capacity, and billing model.

claims.claim_text: The module gives universal thresholds for choosing interconnect over VPN: more than 1 Gbps, less than 5 ms latency, and VPN below 100 Mbps.
claims.anchor_text: **Use interconnect** when: >1 Gbps sustained traffic, <5ms latency required, or compliance demands a private path. **Use VPN** for <100 Mbps, non-critical, or DR-only traffic.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **Use interconnect** when workloads need predictable private connectivity, validated latency, high sustained throughput, or compliance controls that VPN cannot satisfy. **Use VPN** for lower-criticality, bursty, lab, or disaster-recovery paths where internet variability is acceptable.
claims.rationale: The exact thresholds are rules of thumb, not universal technical limits.

claims.claim_text: AWS Direct Connect dedicated connections support 1, 10, 100, and 400 Gbps port speeds, while hosted connections range from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps.
claims.rationale: AWS Direct Connect connection options list the dedicated and hosted connection speed ranges.

claims.claim_text: Inbound data transfer into AWS over Direct Connect is $0.00 per GB in all locations.
claims.rationale: The AWS Direct Connect pricing page directly states inbound data transfer pricing.

claims.claim_text: AWS Direct Connect supports MACsec on 10, 100, and 400 Gbps dedicated connections at select PoPs, and 100/400 Gbps use GCM-AES-XPN-256 with XPN.
claims.rationale: AWS Direct Connect MACsec documentation lists supported speeds and cipher suite requirements.

claims.claim_text: AWS Direct Connect SiteLink routes traffic between Direct Connect locations over the AWS backbone without transiting an AWS Region.
claims.rationale: AWS Prescriptive Guidance describes SiteLink routing between Direct Connect locations without entering AWS Regions.

claims.claim_text: AWS Transit Gateway supports a maximum burst bandwidth of 50 Gbps per VPC, Direct Connect gateway, or peered Transit Gateway connection.
claims.anchor_text: AWS Transit Gateway supports a maximum burst bandwidth of 50 Gbps per VPC, Direct Connect gateway, or peered Transit Gateway connection.
claims.suggested_rewrite: AWS Transit Gateway bandwidth limits and burst behavior are quota-controlled and change over time, so capacity planning should use the current Transit Gateway quotas page.
claims.rationale: Current AWS quota wording no longer safely supports this exact 50 Gbps statement.

claims.claim_text: Azure ExpressRoute standard circuits range from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps, and ExpressRoute Direct supports 10, 100, and 400 Gbps ports with availability constraints.
claims.rationale: Microsoft ExpressRoute Direct documentation lists direct port speeds and circuit SKU ranges.

claims.claim_text: ExpressRoute has Local, Standard, and Premium SKUs; Global Reach links ExpressRoute circuits; Global Reach data transfer is billed separately and not covered by Unlimited Data.
claims.rationale: Microsoft cost planning documentation states Global Reach data transfer is charged per GB separately.

claims.claim_text: Azure Virtual WAN hub router supports up to 50 Gbps, default 2 routing infrastructure units provide 3 Gbps and 2,000 VMs, and P2S VPN aggregate throughput can scale to 200 Gbps.
claims.rationale: Azure Virtual WAN overview and hub settings documentation cover router throughput, default capacity, and gateway throughput.

claims.claim_text: GCP Dedicated Interconnect can bundle up to eight 100 Gbps links into a LAG for 800 Gbps.
claims.anchor_text: GCP Dedicated Interconnect links are available at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps; up to 8 links can be bundled in a Link Aggregation Group (LAG) for up to 800 Gbps.
claims.suggested_rewrite: GCP Dedicated Interconnect links are available at 10 Gbps or 100 Gbps, and aggregate capacity depends on the current Cloud Interconnect circuit and LAG limits.
claims.rationale: Current Google Cloud quotas describe lower per-connection bundle limits than the stated 800 Gbps.

claims.claim_text: GCP Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments support 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps, and Network Connectivity Center provides hub-and-spoke connectivity with BGP route exchange.
claims.rationale: Google Cloud Interconnect and Network Connectivity Center documentation cover Partner Interconnect capacities and NCC route exchange.

claims.claim_text: AWS Interconnect - multicloud is still a November 2025 preview with free 1 Gbps AWS-GCP links, targeting 100 Gbps at GA, and Azure has no firm GA date as of early 2026.
claims.anchor_text: Direct, backbone-to-backbone multicloud connectivity eliminates intermediary colocation complexity. AWS Interconnect – multicloud (in partnership with Google Cloud) entered preview in November 2025, offering 1 Gbps connections during preview at no cost across five AWS–GCP region pairs. It targets 100 Gbps at general availability. While Azure is announced as a future partner, it has no firm GA date as of early 2026. Correspondingly, GCP Cross-Cloud Interconnect supports direct private connections to AWS through this same partnership, but the Azure topology remains ambiguously documented and lacks a confirmed deployment timeline.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Direct, provider-managed multicloud connectivity can reduce colocation complexity, but its partners, regions, bandwidths, status, and pricing change quickly; verify current AWS and Google Cloud documentation before designing around it.
claims.rationale: AWS Interconnect - multicloud reached GA in April 2026, so the preview-specific details are stale.

claims.claim_text: Submariner is a CNCF Sandbox project accepted on April 28, 2021 that enables direct networking between Pods and Services in different Kubernetes clusters.
claims.rationale: The CNCF project page states Submariner's function, Sandbox maturity, and acceptance date.

claims.claim_text: Submariner handles cross-cluster DNS, encrypted tunnels, service discovery, and is CNI-agnostic.
claims.rationale: The Submariner architecture documentation is the primary source, but submariner.io is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: Submariner requirements include non-overlapping pod/service CIDRs, routable gateway nodes, UDP 500 and 4500, and supported CNIs such as Calico, Flannel, Canal, and OVN-Kubernetes.
claims.rationale: Submariner deployment docs are the appropriate primary source, but the domain is off-allowlist.

claims.claim_text: The latest stable Submariner release is v0.23.1, released March 12, 2026.
claims.anchor_text: The latest stable Submariner release is v0.23.1, released on March 12, 2026.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Pin the Submariner version you have validated for the lab, and check the current Submariner release notes before copying install commands.
claims.rationale: Submariner release listings now show a newer v0.24.0 release, making the 'latest' claim stale.

claims.claim_text: Submariner uses a broker for service-discovery metadata exchange, encrypted tunnels for pod-to-pod traffic, and Lighthouse DNS for cross-cluster name resolution.
claims.rationale: The official Submariner architecture page documents Broker and Lighthouse behavior, but submariner.io is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: Cilium ClusterMesh in Cilium 1.19.x provides pod-to-pod and service connectivity across clusters, and the default maximum connected clusters is 255.
claims.rationale: Cilium's official ClusterMesh documentation directly supports the connectivity and default limit, but docs.cilium.io is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: Linkerd supports hierarchical, flat, and federated multi-cluster service models.
claims.anchor_text: Linkerd multi-cluster connectivity has been available since Linkerd 2.8 (June 2020), supporting hierarchical (gateway-based), flat (pod-to-pod), and federated service models.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Linkerd has a multi-cluster mode based on gateway/service mirroring; verify the current release and artifact channel before choosing it for production.
claims.rationale: The topology taxonomy is not directly supported by the Linkerd 2.8 announcement and should be removed unless sourced.

claims.claim_text: As of February 2024, the Linkerd open-source project no longer publishes stable release artifacts; Buoyant provides stable artifacts.
claims.rationale: The Linkerd releases page directly states this, but linkerd.io is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: Istio supports multicluster deployment models including multi-primary and primary-remote.
claims.span_hint: line 237 | Unified Service Mesh with Istio
claims.rationale: Istio's multicluster installation docs list multi-primary and primary-remote topologies.

claims.claim_text: Istio ambient multi-network multicluster reached beta in March 2026 while single-network multicluster remains alpha.
claims.span_hint: line 237 | Unified Service Mesh with Istio
claims.anchor_text: Istio Ambient mesh multi-cluster support (multi-network topology) reached beta status in March 2026; single-network multicluster remains alpha.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Istio 1.29 promoted ambient multi-network multicluster support to beta; single-network multicluster remained alpha in the corresponding Istio announcement.
claims.rationale: The beta announcement was tied to Istio 1.29 in February 2026, so the March date is not accurate.

claims.claim_text: Istio's latest stable release is v1.29.1 from March 10, 2026.
claims.span_hint: line 237 | Unified Service Mesh with Istio
claims.anchor_text: Istio's latest stable release is v1.29.1 (March 10, 2026).
claims.suggested_rewrite: Check the current Istio supported releases page before pinning a version in lab instructions.
claims.rationale: Istio 1.30.0 was announced on May 18, 2026, so this latest-release claim is stale.

claims.claim_text: Without a shared root CA, Istio sidecars in different clusters cannot verify certificates and all cross-cluster traffic fails with 503.
claims.span_hint: line 262 | Unified Service Mesh with Istio
claims.anchor_text: A shared root CA is required for cross-cluster mTLS. Without it, sidecars in different clusters cannot verify each other's certificates and all cross-cluster traffic fails with 503 errors even though network connectivity works.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A shared root CA is required for cross-cluster mTLS; without shared trust, application connectivity can fail even when the underlying network path is healthy.
claims.rationale: The shared-trust requirement is real, but the universal 'all traffic fails with 503' symptom is over-specific.

claims.claim_text: Gatekeeper enforces Kubernetes policies using Open Policy Agent and CRD-based constraints.
claims.rationale: The Gatekeeper repository describes it as a Kubernetes policy controller using OPA.

claims.claim_text: WireGuard was included in Linux 5.6, released in March 2020.
claims.rationale: The Linux v5.6 release tag provides the release reference for the kernel version.

claims.claim_text: Linus Torvalds called WireGuard a 'work of art' compared to IPsec, and WireGuard's 4,000 lines versus IPsec's 400,000 dramatically reduces attack surface.
claims.anchor_text: Linus Torvalds called it a "work of art" compared to IPsec. At ~4,000 lines of code versus IPsec's ~400,000, its attack surface is dramatically smaller.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Its kernel integration made WireGuard a mainstream Linux VPN option, but avoid treating unsourced code-size comparisons as a security metric.
claims.rationale: The quote and exact code-size/attack-surface comparison need primary sourcing and are not safe as written.

claims.claim_text: AWS Direct Connect locations are not AWS datacenters; they are colocation facilities such as Equinix and CoreSite with fiber patching in a meet-me room.
claims.anchor_text: **AWS Direct Connect locations are not AWS datacenters.** They are colocation facilities (Equinix, CoreSite). Your router connects to an AWS router via a physical fiber patch cable in a shared "meet-me room."
claims.suggested_rewrite: **AWS Direct Connect locations are physical interconnection sites.** Depending on the location and partner model, your network reaches AWS through a cross-connect or partner circuit to AWS equipment.
claims.rationale: The absolute 'not AWS datacenters' wording is too broad because AWS documentation lists multiple location models.

claims.claim_text: AWS Interconnect - multicloud preview launched in November 2025 and provides native 1 Gbps tunnels over the backbone.
claims.anchor_text: **AWS Interconnect – multicloud preview launched in November 2025.** By providing native 1 Gbps multicloud tunnels directly over the backbone, it proves native cloud-to-cloud integrations are expanding.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **AWS Interconnect - multicloud moved quickly from preview to GA.** Treat cloud-to-cloud interconnect status, regions, partner support, and bandwidth as live design inputs that must be checked before implementation.
claims.rationale: The preview framing is stale after AWS announced GA in April 2026.

claims.claim_text: Submariner was created by Rancher Labs, is now associated with SUSE, and supports IPsec and WireGuard cable drivers.
claims.rationale: The Submariner project site and related project docs are the primary sources, but submariner.io is not allowlisted.

claims.claim_text: Istio v1.29.1 is the latest stable release and locality-aware load balancing reduces cross-cluster traffic by 60-80% in typical deployments.
claims.anchor_text: **Istio's latest stable v1.29.1** (released March 10, 2026) natively understands locality. Its locality-aware load balancing prefers local endpoints over remote ones automatically, reducing cross-cluster traffic by 60-80% in typical deployments.
claims.suggested_rewrite: **Istio supports locality-aware traffic behavior.** Verify the current Istio release and test locality settings against your own traffic patterns before assuming a specific cross-cluster reduction.
claims.rationale: The latest-version claim is stale and the 60-80% reduction is an unsupported benchmark.

claims.claim_text: Tunnel encapsulation adds 50-70 bytes and tunnel interfaces should use MTU 1400.
claims.anchor_text: | Ignoring MTU in tunnels | Encapsulation adds 50-70 bytes | Set MTU to 1400 on tunnel interfaces |
claims.suggested_rewrite: | Ignoring MTU in tunnels | Encapsulation reduces usable payload size | Calculate and test MTU/MSS for the selected tunnel, path, and provider |
claims.rationale: The byte overhead and 1400 MTU recommendation vary by protocol, cipher, provider, and path.

claims.claim_text: Private networks should not be implicitly trusted; private networks can be compromised.
claims.rationale: NIST SP 800-207 states that no implicit trust should be granted based solely on physical or network location.

notes: No on-premises/resilience citation pool exists in docs/citation-pools. Code blocks, Mermaid diagrams, exercises, and quiz answers were skipped per instructions. Live checks found several stale 'latest' claims: Submariner v0.24.0 is newer than v0.23.1, Istio 1.30.0 was announced after 1.29.1, and AWS Interconnect - multicloud reached GA after the preview language in the module.
